overview.heading: What is MBBS?
paragraphs: MBBS is the main undergraduate medical degree in India for students who want to become doctors. It usually takes 5.5 years: 4.5 years of academic study and 1 year of compulsory rotating internship in a hospital, where students learn under supervision and work with patients. The course is designed to build the knowledge and habits needed for safe medical practice, not just exam success.

The course is science-heavy and practical. Students study subjects like anatomy, physiology, pharmacology, pathology, microbiology, and clinical medicine, then use that learning in wards, clinics, labs, and emergency settings. It suits students who are comfortable with biology, steady study routines, careful observation, and following procedures closely. Communication also matters, because doctors must listen to patients, explain clearly, and work with senior doctors and other health workers.

After MBBS, a graduate cannot practise independently without completing the required internship and then registering with the relevant medical authority. Many doctors later choose further training or specialisation, which changes the kind of work they do and can change how much they earn. The degree is a starting point for a long medical career, not the end of training.

snapshot.data_note: Pay in India changes a lot by city, employer, department, experience, and whether the doctor is in a hospital, clinic, teaching role, or further training. A single figure cannot describe every MBBS graduate because earnings rise over time and differ widely between entry-level roles and more specialised or senior posts.

salary.note: An MBBS doctor in India is commonly shown around 730000 per year, with reported ranges from about 50000 to 1320000 per year. Freshers and doctors in smaller hospitals or training roles may be near the lower end, while doctors with more experience or in better-paying institutions can earn more.

caution.heading: Good to know before choosing MBBS
points: MBBS is not just classroom science; it includes long clinical hours, hospital duties, and regular contact with sick or distressed patients.
The degree alone does not make someone a fully independent doctor; the internship and registration step still come after graduation.
Early-career pay can be modest compared with the length and intensity of the course, and salaries vary sharply by workplace and location.

curriculum.assessment_methods: University theory exams, practical/viva examinations, internal assessments, clinical postings, and compulsory rotatory internship completion.
curriculum.learning_activities: Lectures, dissection and laboratory work, small-group tutorials, ward rounds, bedside case work, community medicine postings, skills-lab practice, and supervised internship rotations.

parent_corner.intro: MBBS suits a student who likes Biology, can handle a long and structured study path, and is comfortable with patient-facing work. Families should look beyond marks and ask whether the student can stay steady under pressure, revise science regularly, and cope with hospital routines, blood, illness, and direct interaction with people. The course is demanding because it combines classroom learning, labs, ward work, and a compulsory internship. It is also a serious time commitment, so planning matters from Class 11 onward. In India, the main admission route is the medical entrance pathway, and after graduation there is still a registration step before practice. Parents can help by checking the student’s interest in care work, their tolerance for hard study, and whether they want to continue into specialisation later.
questions: Does my child genuinely enjoy Biology and helping people, or only the idea of becoming a doctor?
Can they manage a long course with regular revision and hospital-based training?
Are they prepared for the admission competition and the study pressure that comes with it?
Do they understand that MBBS is the start of medical training, not the end of it?
Would they prefer a shorter course with less clinical intensity, or is this the right fit?
Can the family support the time, cost, and years of training involved?
